Many years ago, One long night at the law library, I stumbled on a milestone court case out of Texas from the 1800's. It looked like it was one of the milestone cases that started eroding the 2nd amendment. And now -- we have forgotten the case and we are applying it just the opposite of what was intended!

From what I recall, the case was dealing with a new law that was supposed to more clearly define the common law "rule of ambush". The idea was that if a person ambushed you, then that was never fair. Drawing a hidden dagger was wrong. Well, springing a hidden gun on someone and shooting them also came to be considered a wrongful ambush. The person who got shot would have been more careful, not to pick a fight, if he could have seen that his adversary had a gun in the first place.

The court case, of enough significance to have a written opinion, was about a twist in the application of the new law that better defined the rule of ambush in the context of guns. The case revolved around a man and his wife, in a horse drawn buggy. The man had his gun in the stow box in the buggy. Under the new law, he was "concealing" his gun -- which technically was a violation of the new law, regardless of whether he was ambushing somebody or not!

At that time, there was no connection between banning guns and concealing guns -- it was simply that it was wrong to conceal a gun around others. Had the man and his wife kept the gun out of the stow box, they would not have been violating the new law meant to prevent folks from getting ambushed.

How this translated into it becoming illegal to carry a gun in public I do not yet know. Forty years ago, in the State of Michigan, it was still legal to carry a gun, but not legal to conceal. By the 1970's, the small leather strap holding you gun in your holster was technically considered concealing the gun, making having the gun illegal, even if the gun and holster were in full view! So, if your strap was not snapped the police were told that they should not arrest -- but if the strap was snapped then arrest. By the 21st Century, it is not clear how we turned everything 180 degrees and made "open carry" "illegal". And, so silly, how we now require a CHL -- which effectively defeats the original purpose of the law against concealing a weapon in public!!

If anyone has any comments on this, especially if you know of the old court cases, very welcome to add comments.
